utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Mr. Registrar, may I ask you to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-02-60-A, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. May I ask Mr. Blagojevic and Mr. Jokic if they can hear me and follow the proceedings through the translation. THE APPELLANT BLAGOJEVIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you, Your Honour. THE APPELLANT JOKIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I hear and I can follow. Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. We now call for appearances. For the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned counsel. Appearing for the Prosecution is myself, Norman Farrell, and with me is co-counsel, Ms. Marie-Ursula Kind, Mr. Matteo Costi, Ms. Antoinette Issa, and our case manager today is Ms. Lourdes Galicia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. And for the Defence of Mr. Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, representing Mr. Vidoje Blagojevic, I am Vladimir Domazet, attorney-at-law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. For Mr. Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Peter Murphy for Dragan Jokic. I have with me my legal consultant, Ms. Virginia Lindsay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Now, this is the appeals hearing in the case of the Prosecutor against Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic. I will briefly summarise the appeals which are pending before the Appeals Chamber in the manner in which we'll proceed today. The appeals deal with crimes committed in the immediate aftermath of the take-over of the Srebrenica safe area by the Army of Republika Srpska, VRS, between 6 and 11 July 1995, and with the role played in these events by the Bratunac and Zvornik Brigades of the Drina Corps of the VRS, and in particular, by two of their respective officers at the time, Colonel Vidoje Blagojevic and Major Dragan Jokic. Blagojevic, Jokic, and the Prosecution appealed from a judgement rendered on 17 January 2005 by Trial Chamber I, composed of Judge Liu, presiding and Judges Vassylenko and Argibay. The Trial Chamber found Blagojevic guilty on charges of complicity in genocide, Count 1B; aiding and abetting murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war, Count 4; and aiding and abetting murder, Count 3; persecutions, Count 5; and other inhumane acts, forcible transfer, Count 6, as crimes against humanity. The Trial Chamber sentenced Blagojevic to a single sentence of imprisonment for 18 years. The Trial Chamber found Jokic guilty on charges of aiding and abetting murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war, Count 4; and of aiding and abetting extermination, Count 2; murder, Count 3; and persecutions through murder, Count 5, as crimes against humanity. The Trial Chamber sentenced Jokic to a single sentence of imprisonment for nine years. The Prosecution filed its notice of appeal on 23 February 2005. Blagojevic was granted two further extensions of time and filed his notice of appeal on 31 May 2005. Jokic filed his first notice of appeal on 23 February 2005, followed by a mandate notice of appeal on 25th February 2005, 1st December 2005, then 6 July 2006. I will now briefly summarise their grounds of appeal. Blagojevic brings eight grounds of appeal. In Ground 1, Blagojevic alleges that he was denied to the right of counsel of his choice and the result of a fair trial. Under Ground 2, Blagojevic submits that the Trial Chamber committed several errors of fact resulting in his convictions. In Ground 3, Blagojevic further challenges the Trial Chamber's fact on findings and appealing his convictions for aiding and abetting murder as a crime against humanity and that's a violation of the laws and customs of war, based on the killing of more than 50 Bosnian Muslim men in and around the Vuk Karadzic school in Bratunac. Ground 4 alleges errors relating to his criminal responsibility for forcible transfer. And Ground 5, for persecution. Ground 6 alleges errors relating to his conviction for complicity in genocide. And Ground 7 alleges errors in connection to aiding and abetting. Finally, Ground 8 concerns his appeal from sentence. Jokic brings seven grounds of appeal. Under his first and second Grounds, Jokic alleges that the Trial Chamber erred in law and in fact when it found that he acted with the requisite mens rea for aiding and abetting murder as a violation of the laws and customs of war and murder extermination and persecutions as crimes against humanity. Ground 3 alleges errors relating to the actus reus of aiding and abetting. Under Ground 4, Jokic claims that a legal error was committed in convicting him as an aider and abettor for conduct allegedly confined to ex post facto assistance. Under Ground 5, Jokic submits that the evidence clearly showed an equally probable explanation for his acts consistent with innocence, namely, that his acts and omissions were motivated by public health reasons and therefore lawful. Ground 6 and 7 allege factual errors with respect to Jokic's presence at the duty officer's station in the early hours of 15 July 1995 and his provision of engineering resources and personnel to the Pilica school burial site. The Prosecution brings four grounds of appeal in relation to Blagojevic, two grounds in relation to Jokic, and one ground relating to corroboration of testimony under Rule 92 bis (D). With regard to Blagojevic, Ground 1 alleges that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that Blagojevic did not have knowledge of the mass killings between 12th and 14th July 1995, and consequently erred in finding that he lacked the mens rea for aiding and abetting these crimes. Under Ground 2, the Prosecution asserts that the Trial Chamber erred in fact in finding that Blagojevic did not have the requisite intent to commit forcible transfer as a part of the joint criminal enterprise to forcibly transfer the Bosnian Muslim population out of Srebrenica. Ground 3 alleges that the Trial Chamber erred in law and in fact in finding that Blagojevic was not responsible for the participation of members of the Bratunac Brigade, including Momir Nikolic in the murder operation under Article 7(3). Ground 4 is an appeal relating to Blagojevic's sentence. With regard to Jokic, the Prosecution decided not to proceed with Ground 1. Under Ground 2, the Prosecution alleges that the Trial Chamber erred in fact in concluding that Jokic did not render substantial assistance to the mass executions at the Petkovci school and dam. Ground 3 is an appeal relating to Jokic's sentence. During the hearing, counsel may argue the grounds of appeal in the order they consider most suitable for their presentation, but I would urge them not to repeat just what is in the brief, that the Court is aware of what -- has studied the briefs, so this is not necessary to repeat verbatim or to summarise extensively what is in the brief. I would like to recall the criteria applicable to errors of fact and law alleged on appeal. The appeal is not a trial de novo and the appellants must not merely repeat the case from the trial level; rather, in accordance with Article 24 of the Statute of the Tribunal, the appellants must limit their arguments to alleged errors of law which invalidate the decision or alleged errors of fact occasioning a miscarriage of justice. Additionally, it should be recalled that the appellants have an obligation to provide precise references to materials supporting their arguments on appeal. The hearing will proceed according to the Scheduling Order issued on 10 November 2006. Counsel for Blagojevic will present his submissions this morning until 9.20. From 9.20 to 9.50 we'll hear the response of the Prosecution. Then we have a pause of 30 minutes, then later counsel for Blagojevic will have time to reply for another 20 minutes. And later, we'll proceed with the appeal of Mr. Jokic. And of course, the hearing will continue tomorrow for -- for the remaining issues, in particular, for the appeal of the Prosecution. It would be helpful if the appeal -- to the Chamber if the parties would present their submissions in a precise and clear manner. Judges, of course, may interrupt the parties at any time to ask questions or they may ask questions following each party's submissions or at the end of the hearing. Now, having said this, about the manner in which we will proceed, I would now like to invite counsel for Blagojevic to present submissions in support of his appeal. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. As you are probably aware, Mr. Blagojevic chose me as his Defence counsel for the first time when this was permitted him, and this was after the sentence was handed down, and even after the deadline for the appeal announcement had expired. Then the registrar or the Registry confirmed his choice and officially appointed me as his Defence counsel in this case. I found myself before a very complex assignment, to familiarise myself in a very short period of time with the very delicate and complex case of Srebrenica, with which I had no contact with before. I had to study the judgement and go through over 12.000 pages of the trial transcript and through a large number of evidence and documents in almost 200 binders. I expected, quite rightly I believe, that deadlines would be extended for the submission of appeal briefs, which only partially happened. On the other hand, there was the request of my client, Mr. Blagojevic, to appeal only in relation to the unfair trial that he had because of the imposed Defence team that conducted the proceedings against his will. And without any contact with him from the very beginning of the trial or, more precisely, almost two months before the beginning of the trial, Mr. Blagojevic requested only this to be the subject of his appeal and that I do not deal at all with the other parts of the judgement because he believed that to be pointless. I had the difficult task of gaining the trust in lawyers that he had lost and to convince him that the ground, fair trial, would be the first ground and the main part of his appeal, but that I was bound to also appeal in relation to the rest of the judgement, even if this was not what he wanted. This is what I did, but I did have a lot of time pressures and other limitations. I had to submit the notice of appeal by the 31st of May, 2005, just two months after I took the case, without having the possibility by then to read and review the entire transcript of the trial. I was rejected in my request that the deadline for the response by the Prosecution should start after I have submitted my appeal brief, so that I had to already submit my response to the OTP appeal brief by the 20th of June, even though I was still not in the position to be entirely familiar with the whole case. And then I had to submit the actual appeal brief only seven days after the deadline for the same brief by the Jokic Defence. Because of the way this case was categorised at the lower level and the refusal to acknowledge an additional number of hours in order to familiarise myself with a completely new case, I didn't have the option of having the assistance of a co-counsel. And the legal advisor that I initially asked for and appointed, an attorney with experience as a Defence counsel before this trial, was only a few days after being appointed released from this duty by the Registry, which made my work on the appeal much more difficult. I'm sorry that I had to state all of this before actually moving to my submission, and that I had to use the already limited time on stating this. Vidoje Blagojevic did not have a fair trial. The main issue in the first part of the appeal, that is Ground 1, is whether or not Mr. Blagojevic had a fair trial. Could the trial have been fair when he did not take part in it in any way? From the very beginning until the sentence was handed down, Mr. Blagojevic used every opportunity when he was given the floor to point out this problem, which was that he did not have a proper Defence and that the attorney, Mr. Karnavas, who was his counsel was actually his enemy who was not working in his interest. He wanted to have the right to appoint new lawyers, but this right was granted to him only after the judgement was handed down, so that is almost two full years after the lawyer was dismissed. Throughout this time, Blagojevic was left to his own devices without legal assistance, except during the brief period when he had an independent lawyer but with no effect on the trial itself. The Appeals Chamber did have a part in resolving this problem, but at the very beginning, when both the Trial Chamber and the Appeals Chamber believed that this was a conflict between a lawyer and the accused, which could be resolved in the course of the trial and that there will be trust and confidence established between the two already opposing parties. It's possible that such a position was reached also on the basis of the belief of the Court that the conflict arose just because of the figure of the co-counsel, which was actually the initial reason for the dispute, but it was just the initial reason I note. It can be said that the dispute between Mr. Blagojevic and Mr. Karnavas did begin because of the co-counsel, or let's say that it culminated at that point because, at that point, Mr. Blagojevic felt cheated. At that time, there was never any agreement between him and Mr. Karnavas that Suzana Tomanovic would be co-counsel during the actual trial. Mr. Blagojevic considered her to be an interpreter and associate of Mr. Karnavas, which was beyond dispute at that point in time. This was never actually discussed, and it was quite natural for Mr. Blagojevic to want to have a more experienced lawyer from Serbia as co-counsel with whom he could communicate in his native tongue. He felt that that would be quite important for his defence. Mr. Blagojevic wanted that and he also wanted to personally see and meet the future co-counsel. This was, unfortunately, not possible, not even when that lawyer came to The Hague for that specific purpose. Mr. Karnavas, himself, reacted in a very ugly manner, charging the colleague of his whom he met in Belgrade of not only being incompetent, although we are talking about a lawyer who has had a career of many years in the profession, but he actually called him a plain clown. Something like this could not lead to mutual trust and confidence between the accused and Mr. Karnavas, and it actually made the crisis in their relationship even more serious. Even had Mr. Karnavas's objections to that attorney been correct, he did not allow Mr. Blagojevic the possibility of suggesting another attorney from Serbia, which was Mr. Blagojevic's express wish. On the contrary, he did everything to have the co-counsel of his own choice appointed, and Mr. Blagojevic expressly opposed this. But Mr. Karnavas wanted the co-counsel he had chosen to remain, and this deepened the crisis in their mutual relations, as was evident in all the subsequent Status Conferences. Mr. Karnavas then stated that he would withdraw from the case if he was not in a position to control the case, that is, to have Mrs. Tomanovic as the exclusive co-counsel. Later on, he rejected any possibility of voluntarily withdrawing from the case and did everything to remain, even at the cost of not having any contact whatsoever with the accused, of representing the defence of an accused who did not want him as his counsel and who took every possible opportunity to state this during the trial to the Trial Chamber. At the Status Conference held on the 27th of March, 2003, Mr. Karnavas, responding to a question from Judge Schomburg, stated that he would not act as Defence counsel without Mrs. Tomanovic. He stated on that occasion and repeated more than once that he would withdraw from the case should that be Mr. Blagojevic's wish, and that it was only up to Mr. Blagojevic to make that choice. However, although Mr. Blagojevic, in his letter of the 7th of April, 2003, expressly dismissed Mr. Karnavas and informed the Registry that he did not wish him to be his Defence counsel under any circumstances, Mr. Karnavas not only changed his position and failed to keep his promise, but on the contrary, not only did he demand that he remain as counsel - although he had been dismissed - but fabricated a false accusation of fee splitting. After the Status Conference held on the 27th of March, 2003, where, in private session, Mr. Blagojevic clearly stated his position and Judge Schomburg stated that he would inform the Registry and the Chamber of all this, the conflict led to a complete breakdown of relations and Mr. Blagojevic's decision to dismiss his Defence team, that is Mr. Karnavas, which he did in a letter dated the 7th of April, 2003. Unfortunately, this letter was not delivered to the Trial Chamber also, as should have been done, and the Trial Chamber learned of this problem only at the start of trial. The Presiding Judge Liu then held this against representatives of the Registry. It is very odd, to put it mildly, that the ex parte session of the Status Conference held on the 27th of March, 2003, was not contained in the transcript obtained by the Defence counsel from the Court. There was only a transcript of the public part of the Status Conference, although according to the transcript, it was interrupted and a continuation was announced after a break, after which a private conference was held. But the transcript of the continuation was not in the case file, and I did not receive it. It was only when I stated this at the Status Conference on that same day that I received from the OTP a transcript of the ex parte Status Conference. However, in May 2003, when the decision on Blagojevic's motion was made, it was evident that all this was threatening the start of trial and that this is what influenced the decision that the accused should not be permitted to appoint another Defence team. However, it is evident that the prevailing conviction was that the conflict between the accused and Mr. Karnavas could and would be straightened out and that there would be a reinstatement of confidence between the two. And this, however, never happened because, in the meantime, Mr. Karnavas, in a submission responding to the request to have an independent counsel appointed, stated clearly in more than one paragraph that he was accusing Mr. Blagojevic of attempted fee splitting. There are as many as nine paragraphs in the motion where Mr. Karnavas gave reasons why he should remain the counsel in spite of his dismissal accusing Mr. Blagojevic of fee splitting. I point this out not only to show that this was the decisive influence on the decision that Mr. Blagojevic should not be permitted the right to choose his own counsel, but that this false and tendentious accusation destroyed any possibility of re-establishing any form of cooperation which would be a prerequisite in this case, in this kind of case. In the press, an article was published under the title "Racket Behind the Walls of Scheveningen" about the Blagojevic case dealing with this accusation which was later proved to be false and fabricated. This serious accusation which was completely untrue and which was fabricated caused Mr. Blagojevic to abide by his decision that Mr. Karnavas was not and could not be his Defence counsel, since Mr. Karnavas had accused him of being a common criminal. And after this false accusation, under no circumstances would he accept Mr. Karnavas as his Defence counsel; on the contrary, he considered him to be his enemy. This was the culmination of the conflict which occurred when Mr. Karnavas falsely and tendentiously accused Mr. Blagojevic of being motivated by fee splitting in their conflict, and fee splitting is an impermissible activity which represents a very serious accusation. Mr. Karnavas did this at a point in time when the decision was to be made as to whether he was to be replaced or not in June 2003, and in Mr. Blagojevic's opinion, this was what decisively influenced the position of the Registry and their decision. However, this false and fabricated accusation also had an influence on Mr. Blagojevic, who after this would not accept any kind of compromise and would under no circumstances accept Mr. Karnavas as his counsel. The fact that this accusation was really false was confirmed by Mr. Karnavas himself, but only a year later when the end of the trial was drawing near. On the 13th of July, 2004, at the Status Conference, he probably hoped that this statement would influence Blagojevic and that he would in this way get Mr. Blagojevic to accept him as his counsel. He stated in nine paragraphs of his motion a year previously something that was completely different. Mr. Blagojevic, as an honourable man with no stain in his life or his career as an officer, could not accept this belated admission of a false accusation and he abided by his position that he could have no contact with the counsel who had been appointed by the Registry against his will. Mr. Blagojevic had no influence on the course of the trial during the Prosecution case; and, which is far worse, he had no influence in the course of the Defence case, which was handled by a team of counsel imposed on him without his knowledge and influence. That is why some witnesses of the so-called Defence were hostile and detrimental to his case. These, however, are details. What is most important is that in the proceedings before this Tribunal and according to the jurisprudence and legal system, the trial could not have been fair because Mr. Blagojevic did not have a proper defence, either during the Prosecution case or, more importantly, during the Defence case. Mr. Blagojevic, unfortunately, was only a silent observer. Not only was it not possible for Blagojevic himself to testify, although he wanted to and still wants to because he was prevented in the manner described. What was especially disastrous for his position during the trial is that he could not influence the choice of witnesses, which Mr. Karnavas did according to criteria only known to him. Is it possible in this system to have a fair trial if the accused has no influence on the choice of witnesses who are supposed to represent his Defence and has no influence on their examination? The only reasonable response is that the trial cannot be fair, regardless of whether the Defence counsel wants it to be fair or not. It is simply impossible to mount a Defence case without the accused participating actively. This is not only due to the choice of witnesses and their examination, although that is the key issue. No less important, however, is the selection of written documents to be tendered into evidence or not tendered into evidence. This is truly not possible without the active participation of the accused. The selection and role of the military expert witness in this case was exceptionally important. This can be seen from the importance attributed to this by the Prosecution, and the voluminous nature of the expert report, as well as the number of days on which the military expert testified. However, although expert witness Schifaneli submitted the report, Mr. Karnavas did not call him to appear. At the very beginning, he locates the Drina Corps as a unit active in North-Eastern Bosnia, which was only one but not the only major mistake made by this witness. The Trial Chamber, however, quoted only this completely erroneous fact in its judgement, even had the expert report been done properly and well, the expert witness should have been called to testify and been examined in the course of the trial. None of this happened, however, and it should be weighed whether the accused did or did not have a fair trial. In spite of all this, if the Registry judged that the trial was fair, then why was the accused allowed to change his Defence team without any new procedures being installed in the course of the time-period needed to file a notice of appeal. The decision of Mr. Blagojevic, or rather, the decision to allow Mr. Blagojevic the choice of new Defence counsel after the end of the trial and the handing down of the judgement was fair, but it was belated because the possibilities in an appeal case are limited. So the fairest solution proposed in his appeal is a new trial, together with the whole group accused for the Srebrenica case who have -- whose trial has not yet begun. Mr. Blagojevic does not fear any possible new evidence which might turn up in that case because he wishes the truth to be established. Mr. Blagojevic still wishes to testify under oath, and this was not possible in the previous trial. Mr. Blagojevic feels that joining his indictment to the currently ongoing trial for Srebrenica and making it possible for him to present his Defence case and testify in person would not only not be detrimental to the other participants in that case, but would also be in the interests of justice because one and the same Trial Chamber would hand down a judgement for all those accused in the Srebrenica case, with the exception of those who are not yet available to the Tribunal. Mr. Blagojevic, as he will probably tell you himself, is not afraid of such a trial or any of the evidence that might turn up and be used in that trial which were not used during his trial. The only thing that he wishes is a fair trial with a Defence counsel of his choice, regardless of the judgement and ultimately handed down. For all the reasons given above and also from what is written in our appeal, the Blagojevic Defence expects, first of all, that this Appeals Chamber will accept the first and main ground of appeal relating to the unfair trial of the accused Blagojevic and that it will not have to review and decide on the other grounds of appeal by the Defence and the Prosecution. The Defence expects this ground of appeal to be excepted, which would make it possible for the accused Blagojevic to have a new trial, either alone or with the group of accused according to the Srebrenica indictment. He could join then the other accused being at trial and the same Trial Chamber then would be able to decide on all the existing evidence submitted, both by the Prosecution and the Defence, regardless of the earlier, the previous, case. This would be the proper and fair manner to hand down a judgement in the case of the accused Blagojevic with full respect of his basic rights, his right to a defence in which he has trust and confidence and his right to a fair trial. The right to a fair trial is something that Colonel Blagojevic, the then-commander of the Bratunac Brigade, has a right to in order to be able to show that he's not guilty for the tragedy and the victims in Srebrenica; that he was in command of over 2.000 members of the brigade; and that none of them was charged, either here in The Hague or in Sarajevo, with the exception of Momir Nikolic, who as a security officer was in that period not acting under the command of Colonel Blagojevic but as part of and according to the plan of execution of counter-intelligence tasks, according to orders of the security organ of a higher command. Only the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, Colonel Blagojevic, has been charged before this Tribunal, who, during the Krivaja operation, was in command of the brigade and was mostly in Pribicevac, which was his forward command post; who during the days in question, never saw General Mladic, even though the general not only came to Bratunac but had meetings there. Colonel Blagojevic did not attend any of those meetings, while he only saw the commander of the Drina Corps, General Krstic, only once and that was on the 11th of July, 1995, sometime after 2200 hours. Colonel Blagojevic was carrying out assignments given to him during those days, and he was prepared to go into combat with his brigade on the lines to which he was assigned, not only were there no combat actions by his brigade because of the way the situation developed, and they did not happen to see a single enemy soldier, never mind kill or arrest one. They didn't have any contact whatsoever with civilians either. Due to all of the above, Colonel Blagojevic would like to have a fair trial in which he's prepared to testify himself and he expects to be given justice and he would like to present the truth for which he has been fighting for several years here. For all of the above reasons today, in the appeal submission, I submit that the trial -- that the Appeals Chamber should acknowledge and accept Vidoje Blagojevic's appeal and enable him a new and fair trial. Thank you, Your Honours. I have completed my oral submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. You would have more time allotted to you. Is your intention to conclude here your submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. If possible, if I can have a minute more in my response, that would mean a lot to me, when I submit my response, but for now, I have finished my oral submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. So shall we take it that for the remaining grounds of appeal, you just refer to what you wrote in your brief? Is that correct? For the time being and with reserve -- without prejudice to what you may say during the reply, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Your Honour, that is the case, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, I'm not quite clear about where you stand on the appeal. You have given one reply to the President a moment ago, but in your argument two minutes ago, you said the Defence does not expect the Appeals Chamber to review other grounds of appeal, and you have asked only for a new trial together with other Srebrenica defendants. I would like you to please be a bit more precise as to whether you, the Defence, maintains the grounds of appeal which appear in the briefs that you have presented to the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I stand by all the appeal grounds that are stated in the appeals brief. I would just like to explain. My position is that I consider that if the Appeals Chamber were to accept the first ground of appeal, deciding on a new trial, then there would be no need to look at the other grounds of appeal of the Defence and of the Prosecution because there would be a new trial. Of course, if this should not be the case, then I would like to have all the grounds of appeal reviewed. That would be the explanation of my position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: But you realise, of course, that this is -- you only have this opportunity today and tomorrow to argue on behalf of your client, and by limiting your argument today to just one area, haven't you been sort of putting all your eggs in one basket? Also, would you be prepared to reply to questions from the Bench on other grounds of appeal?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour. I understood from what was said that in any case what is stated in the appeal brief is important, and the oral submissions today are limited. And even if I were to discuss each ground of appeal I could here at this time only say a couple of sentences about each one, and this is why I restricted myself, also in accordance with the wishes of my client, to putting forth in as much details as possible the first ground of appeal. As I said, I abide by the grounds because, primarily, I believe that Ground 1 is well-founded and I believe that it should be granted. If this should not be the case, and I'm not prepared to go into this right now, I am of course prepared to respond to the other grounds of appeal, of course, after the response by the Prosecution and then my response to their submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Your position is quite clear. I think Judge Guney wanted to have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I understand there is no interpretation. Is there a problem with the translation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There is no problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand French perfectly. It's my mother tongue on my mother's side, anyway -- and French, it's my mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Maybe if we have interpretation, Judge Guney, you may go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me resume. I said that during your submission on the 11th of July, 1993 [as interpreted], Mr. Blagojevic was prepared to fight with those people under his command. He waited the entire day and never entered the town because the second sentence had changed. Would you have the kindness to specify what these change and circumstances were all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I'm going to respond in the language that Mr. Blagojevic understands, and it was his wish that I only use that language today. I will try to explain that. Mr. Blagojevic had orders and tasks that -- according to which he assigned his companies to positions, and he was at the command post in Pribicevac; that is close to Srebrenica. He was supposed to move to Srebrenica from there. However, it came about that the use of his units was not necessary and that his units had no contact with the opposing side, and at that time he was not aware why this happened, probably because the military forces pulled out from a different side, the military forces of the 28th Bosnia and Herzegovina army. They withdrew in a different direction, went towards Tuzla, and that is precisely the axis where most of them were intercepted and where most of them were captured, but not by members of the Bratunac Brigade who were actually on the opposite side. And in that sector, they did not encounter a single enemy soldier, not even a civilian, because this is not a populated area. And that is why I assert in the appeals brief and now that the Bratunac Brigade practically did not participate in the capture of Srebrenica when completely different military and police forces entered the town. The order that he had to search the terrain in front of the positions of his units has nothing to do with what he is being charged with, and that is capturing the soldiers and other things, because his units did not encounter any soldiers that they could capture. So that is the essence of what the Bratunac Brigade was doing at that time. As for how the change of plan came about is something that Colonel Blagojevic does not know and nobody asked anything of him in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Domazet. I think -- oh, Judge Meron, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I have -- Mr. Domazet, I have one or two questions for you. The first one refers to the murders at the Vuk Karadzic school. Assuming that Mr. Blagojevic heard gun-fire and screaming while in Bratunac, how can we not accept the Trial Chamber's findings, suggesting that he knew of the murders. Surely, at a certain point, enough gun-fire and screaming means more than inhumane treatment; it means murder. Please answer, keeping in mind that we can only reverse if no reasonable Trial Chamber could have found knowledge of murder beyond a reasonable doubt. This is my first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as for the prisoners who were in the Vuk Karadzic school, I think that it is clear that these were not prisoners of the Bratunac Brigade. As for the conclusion of the Trial Chamber that Colonel Blagojevic could have heard, as you say, the shooting or, as you say, even the screaming, the moaning, during the night, I am just going to repeat what I stated in the appeals brief, and that is that Colonel Blagojevic was either at the command post in Pribicevac, thus outside Bratunac, or at his own command post, which is quite a distance away from the Vuk Karadzic school, it's in another part of town. The Trial Chamber concluded, quite erroneously in my view, that Blagojevic slept in his apartment, which according to the findings of the Trial Chamber, is closer to the school. It is closer than the command, obviously, and we know that the command was too far to be able to hear the screaming and the moaning. Perhaps the shooting could have been heard, but not the screaming. However, there was no possibility for Mr. Blagojevic to prove the basic thing, and that was that the apartment used by the previous brigade commander was sealed because of some problems of the previous commander and was not in use. Mr. Blagojevic did not enter the apartment. At the time, Mr. Blagojevic slept in his own command, right next to his office, or at the Hotel Fontana. He never slept in the apartment. So from where he was, if there was some screaming, it was impossible to hear; as for the firing, it was something that was happening often at that time. Some witnesses talked about shooting, but not in such a way that this was -- would draw anybody's special attention at the time. The controversial Momir Nikolic, who was a security officer and did participate in various activities in Potocari and Bratunac, had stated that he didn't know about the murders or the killings in the Vuk Karadzic school. He found about them later. If he, as a participant, did not know that there were sporadic killings that night, then it is even less likely that Colonel Blagojevic knew about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. My second and last question is this: In your appeals brief, you note that your client's trial counsel did not make an argument as to sentencing. Did this prejudice your client, and if so, how? In particular, were there other mitigating circumstances that the Trial Chamber would have found if trial counsel had briefed the matter? Could you please enlighten us, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as for the sentencing arguments relating to the actual sentence, no. Perhaps that is erroneous if I said something like that in the appeals brief. Perhaps I had said that it was not possible to speak about anything like that without any contacts with the accused. But Mr. Blagojevic did not want me to discuss the sentence at all in this appeal and to dwell on the sentence as a ground of appeal at all. So I guess that would also apply to the counsel who was imposed on him at the time, Mr. Karnavas. If this is stated in my appeals brief, it does not mean that it is something that it would have any effect on the outcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Domazet. Judge Vaz wants the floor, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would just like to put one question. Can you tell us whether the lack of communication between Mr. Karnavas and Mr. Blagojevic was due to the fact that the latter considered Mr. Karnavas to be his enemy - this is a word you used a while ago - and therefore was not willing to prepare his defence? Or was it that Mr. Karnavas did not want to work with him to prepare the defence of his client, Mr. Blagojevic? If you can explain to us these two problems, whether one can strike a balance here or not, whether this can be explained or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try. I will try, Your Honour, to respond to this point. As I said, the conflict or the dispute between the two of them -- first of all, let me explain. Enemy-like or as an enemy is something that Mr. Blagojevic used several times when he was allowed to speak by the Trial Chamber. It is a word that he used, a term that he used. I tried to explain that the dispute that started first because of the co-counsel appointment, where Mr. Blagojevic was explicitly against the solution suggested by Mr. Karnavas, and then the dispute went on, and it was not -- this was not the only cause for the dispute. As you could see in the Status Conferences, there was a lack of mutual trust, and there was no joint preparation of the Defence, especially when we're talking about the military expert, because this was not even discussed at that point. So I don't know how Mr. Karnavas decided which witnesses and experts to choose for the trial because this was not discussed. Mr. Karnavas could in no way be satisfactory as far as Mr. Blagojevic was concerned, and then what happened happened. Mr. Blagojevic felt that appointing a more experienced lawyer from Belgrade as co-counsel would provide him more of an opportunity to influence and monitor the work of the main Defence counsel, with whom he communicated through an interpreter. And there were problems. But all of these things that happened as a result led to a complete lack of trust and confidence, and this culminated, when in the course of the proceedings, he was quite unjustly charged with fee splitting and then such a charge was a year later denied by Mr. Karnavas, but it led Mr. Blagojevic to conclude that Mr. Karnavas was an enemy and that he did not want to communicate with him in any way, and it led to the things that happened later. I think that had there been a possibility, it would have been good to introduce the question of the Defence after the completion of the Prosecution case and before the start of the Defence case; that would have been a good moment, otherwise this is something that was not actually discussed even though Mr. Blagojevic did try to resolve this at several points during the trial. And that is why we had the situation that only after the handing down of the judgement, Mr. Blagojevic was permitted to have a new lawyer, to appoint a lawyer of his own choice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Domazet. Well, this concludes, I believe, the submissions of -- and the questions concerning Mr. Blagojevic's appeal. We'll have now the response of the Prosecution. I will give the floor for 30 minutes to the Prosecution to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Good morning. Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. As Mr. Domazet has focused his submissions on essentially the first ground of appeal, I suspect that our response will be relatively short and we'll limit our response to that ground of appeal. If there are any comments I can add in relation to the questions that were raised by the Bench, I'll do so and of course in relation to Mr. Domazet's appeal I'm available, as are my co-counsel, to answer any questions. A large part of Mr. Domazet's arguments this morning have been on the issue of what led to the Trial Chamber's decision and subsequently the Appeals Chamber's decision on whether or not his counsel should be withdrawn. The issues pertaining to the cause of the concern and the resulting breakdown between Mr. Blagojevic and his counsel have been fully briefed, argued, and decided upon by the Trial Chamber, and subsequently, in an interlocutory appeal decided on December 15th, 2003, with written decisions on November the 7th, 2003. The issues as to whether counsel should have been withdrawn have been dealt with and resolved by this Appeals Chamber in my respectful submission, and that the cause for -- the alleged cause for the breakdown and the refusal to cooperate was before the Appeals Chamber, including all the material that's been referred to, the transcripts in March 2003, the material in the media that was referred to, and the other material related to the comments by Mr. Karnavas as to the proposed co-counsel. I won't go through those facts, as in my submission those issues have been decided. My submission -- what the Court has to decide on this appeal is whether or not the breakdown in -- and lack of communication throughout the trial has resulted in an unfairness and a miscarriage of justice. We're past the point of deciding whether the withdrawal was the decision not to withdraw was valid or not; that was decided already. What the Appeals Chamber is left with, though, is the somewhat unique circumstances where a trial proceeded without the ability of counsel to consult with his client and without the ability of the client to advise his counsel. But in this case, the Court has found that that arose from his refusal to cooperate or communicate with his counsel, and that that wasn't reasonable -- objectively reasonable or a matter that justified that refusal. Regardless of the cause of the breakdown, the question that must be answered is whether or not, as a result of the breakdown of communications, the trial was rendered unfair. This raises issues not normally associated with an effective assistance of counsel, at least the cases that we've seen before Akayesu and other cases deal with the issue where there is an allegation that counsel wasn't competent. The issue in my submission here is whether or not that competency or effective representation was affected, regardless of the good-will and the efforts of Defence counsel and the willingness to continue to represent him to the best of his ability, but whether or not that lack of communication leads to an unfair trial and, as the standard is set out in Akesiu and miscarriage of justice. The Defence alleges first that the very fact of the breakdown of the communication in and of itself results in an unfair trial and warrants the granting of his appeal. With respect to the breakdown of the communication does not automatically result in an unfair trial. Certainly this Court has to carefully scrutinise the record. Of course this Court will and has to make sure that the trial was fair in light of the unique circumstances that we find ourselves in after the trial is over, but the Court has also recognised that the accused does not have the unilateral right to destroy a relationship with counsel, thereby, in effect, guaranteeing a finding of gross negligence and therefore resulting in his ability to cause a new trial at his own whim. The Appeals Chamber warned against this very result in its decision when it said he did not have the right to unilaterally destroy the trust between himself and counsel. And further, at the end of the Appeals Chamber's decision, the written decision on November 7th, the Appeals Chamber made it clear that he could not proceed to continue to assert a right on the basis of a claim which had no merit. As Defence hasn't gone through them, I won't either, but the review of the witnesses and the documents that the Defence allege, primarily in their written brief, a review of them do not demonstrate that there was ineffective assistance in counsel. Essentially what the Defence has to do on this appeal is show, first of all, what the Defence counsel did which resulted in a miscarriage because of the inability to communicate; or, alternatively, what Defence counsel didn't do because of an inability to communicate. And in my respectful submission, that hasn't been shown. Counsel at trial, as Your Honours are aware, has a wide discretion with how to proceed with a case. And a strategic decision or even a mistake does not necessarily result in gross negligence. That was the specific ruling of this case in the decision of the Prosecutor versus Momir Nikolic, where counsel for Momir Nikolic alleged that counsel at trial was incompetent for failing to put medical records before the Court and the Appeals Chamber found that that wasn't the case, it was a strategic decision, and even if a mistaken one, would not warrant the admission of the evidence on appeal. The second point I wanted to make was that the -- there is a silence from the appellant's counsel as to what the actual prejudice was or where the miscarriage of justice is. Though there's reference to witnesses, for example, Momir Nikolic's testimony, and other aspects of the Defence case, the Defence hasn't clearly demonstrated where that resulted in a miscarriage in the trial record. In relation to the violation of the accused's rights to testify, I think it's fairly clear that the Trial Chamber made extensive efforts to ensure that his rights were actually protected. They wanted to ensure that he was properly informed, that any decision to testify or not to testify was voluntary. And in the end of the day what happened is that the counsel -- the accused, based on the conditions that were required, both by the Trial Chamber but by the Rules, declined to exercise the right to counsel in a manner which accorded with the Rules and the Trial Chamber's decision. At the end of the day, just simply to reiterate, that this is not an issue of whether or not the withdrawal was a correct decision -- or the decision not to withdrawal was correct or not; that's been decided. The issue is whether in the unique circumstances of this case there was an unfair trial. The fact that there was not communication does not automatically result. The Court is fully aware, if you review the filings, primarily the confidential filings or some of the ex parte filings, that there was extensive consultation prior to trial up until the time when there was the final breakdown in April of 2003. There was discussions between Defence counsel and client. There was strategic decisions made. There was discussions about the Prosecution witnesses and the Prosecution witness list. The Defence response to the Prosecution's pre-trial brief wherein the Defence position and its response to the Prosecution's theory of the case, that was all done prior to the breakdown of the communication. And Defence counsel was clearly in a position to know what the position was of his client and how they intended to respond to the Prosecution's theory and facts. The appellant now has been represented by counsel, who appears to have his full trust and full communication. The present counsel with full consultation with his client has put forward all the arguments which both in counsel and the appellant's view demonstrate why the trial was unfair. The Appeals Chamber will see upon a review of these arguments that none of them demonstrate an ineffective representation at trial. Further, this Tribunal has the unique mechanism of Rule 115 and the jurisprudence of this Tribunal has recognised that the exception to the availability of evidence at trial, one of those exceptions is gross negligence of counsel. And that even if the evidence was available at trial, if it was the result of gross negligence of counsel, it will be considered by the Court for admission. Despite claiming that there was evidence that was not called and being critical of the evidence that was called, despite having the opportunity to consult with his client, claiming that there were things that could have been done or were not done over the two-year period there was no consultation, I note that there's not one piece of additional evidence that's been submitted that generates from the renewed consultation between client and counsel. There are no additional witnesses brought. There are no new documents found. In fact, there's no new factual arguments raised that were not raised in essence at the trial. Lastly, in relation to the right of the accused to testify, as I've indicated, it's not an issue of whether he -- the client is right, it's an issue of whether he -- the client to exercise his right. He was placed in the same position as any other accused who wishes to testify. And the fact that he refused to testify according to the Rules and the procedures established by the Trial Chamber because he didn't want to be examined by counsel, does not prove that the right to counsel has been violated; and, more significantly, it does not make competent counsel incompetent. As there's been no demonstration of the right to effective representation at trial that has been denied or resulted in a miscarriage of justice, it's submitted that this ground of appeal should be denied. In light of the fact that there's been no other submissions on substance on the remaining grounds of appeal, the Prosecution does not make any submissions in that regard. If I may, with leave of the President, address a few of the issues that arose in the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all, obviously, as Mr. Domazet has relied on his brief, the Prosecution does so as well. Secondly, there is a question by Judge Meron, and, Your Honour, I will try to look at this and address it more fully, but I may have either misunderstood your question or probably more likely misunderstood the judgement. So I would like to respond to the issue you raised about surely at some point in time the evidence that there was sufficient gun-fire in the Vuk Karadzic school would have resulted in, clearly, knowledge that there were murders that were happening in Bratunac. If I understood your question correctly, and I apologise if I haven't, my understanding -- the implication of your question is that he was not found guilty of the murders in the Vuk Karadzic school and that if he at some point in time, if there was sufficient evidence of the gun-fire from which you could infer knowledge, it means that there would be enough evidence for murder, is -- am I misunderstanding your question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Just to make it completely clear, let me repeat the question as I asked it of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Assuming that Blagojevic heard gun-fire and screaming while in Bratunac, how can we not accept the Trial Chamber's findings in paragraph so-and-so, suggesting that he new of the murders? Surely at a certain point, enough gun-fire and screaming means more than inhumane treatment; it means murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Then I misunderstood your question. The Trial Chamber did as you indicated and as is found at paragraphs 784, 785, and 786 did find him guilty of the murders. Thank you. My apologies. The second issue that was raised by Judge Vaz, and as well, I hope I understood it correctly. Judge Vaz raised a question which resulted in an assessment of whether or not how the Court was to balance between whether or not Blagojevic was not willing to work with Defence counsel and therefore not willing to prepare with him; or whether or not it was the Defence counsel Karnavas who did not want to meet him. If I understand Your Honour's question correctly, the record, the factual record, demonstrates that the Defence counsel was willing to work with the accused during trial and that it was the refusal of the accused that prevented that from happening and prevented the preparation right up until the point in time when Defence counsel -- I'm sorry, right up until the point in time where the accused at the time was asked whether he was willing to testify in, I think, it was July 2004 and then again in September 2004. The Court requested Mr. Karnavas to speak with his client, which he was willing to do, and approached him on at least two occasions to discuss with him his right to testify. And subsequently, in a closed session ex parte at the time, I recall, session, Defence counsel specifically stated on the record in front of his client that his advice to his client was not to testify and not to exercise that right. That was his legal advice. So if I understood your question correctly, the Court attempted to strike a balance in ensuring that whenever necessary and whenever the Court felt it was absolutely necessary that they instructed consultation and that Defence counsel was willing to do so, not only when the Trial Chamber requested it, but on an ongoing basis. That was on the factual record, if that addresses your question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was a question which I asked. You have answered my question. I just wanted to know what Defence counsel felt about this. Thank you, Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification, Judge Vaz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Farrell, this matter came on interlocutory appeal to the Appeals Chamber. Now, I suppose this could be said: If an accused person is not getting on with his counsel, then the Appeals Chamber may say, Well, look it's your fault and you either take existing counsel or you can self represent. Now, the Appeals Chamber, we know, has a competence -- well, a Chamber has a competence in exceptional circumstances to say to an accused person, Well, you will be represented by counsel even if you do not have any communications with that counsel, but I take it that's in very special and restricted circumstances. What happens here is this, if I apprehend correctly the circumstances, the position is that the Appeals Chamber would have said to Mr. Blagojevic, Well, it's all your fault. That's the counsel assigned to you, and you take him and I suppose leave him -- or leave him. But did the Appeals Chamber go on to say that even if you do not have any confidence in that counsel, the counsel may speak on your behalf? There's a fine distinction between a situation in which a Trial Chamber may exceptionally say to an accused, Look, that's your counsel, he will speak on your behalf even if you do not speak to him. And a case in which the Appeals Chamber doesn't say that, what happens afterwards is that there is a lack of communications between counsel and client and counsel still speaks in court for the client. Is that permissible, Mr. Farrell?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you for your question, Judge Shahabuddeen. The simple answer is: Yes. If in the circumstances, the Chamber's decision is one which results in saying: There's no basis for the withdrawal, but doesn't go further and say: As a result, we impose counsel and he must act on your behalf. Then what the Trial Chamber is left with in this case is either he seeks to represent himself or the Trial Chamber has to indicate that counsel is to remain. In this case, the Trial Chamber made it abundantly clear in some of its rulings, including one of its rulings at the end in relation to the right to testify, that the accused, during trial, had indicated that he did not want to represent himself. That being the case, and in light of the decision of both this Appeals Chamber and the Trial Chamber, that counsel have an obligation to stay on the record to defend the client, then at that stage the only choice of the Trial Chamber would be to maintain the counsel which was essentially imposed as a result of the decision but not imposed because of the decision directly, if that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, President. Mr. Farrell, you spoke of strategic decisions by the counsel which should not be second-guessed, if I may paraphrase you. You heard my question to the Defence regarding absence of sentencing arguments. Now, the Rules provide, as you know, that if a party decides to have closing arguments, then sentencing submissions are no longer optional. What I would like to know from you is: Do you think that by not making any submissions on sentencing, Mr. Blagojevic's interests may have been prejudiced somehow?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: First of all, I'm not familiar with the record in terms of the actual oral submissions. I appreciate -- I will check on this, and I apologise I wasn't aware. I know the closing brief may be that way. In the circumstances of this case when the -- to answer your question: No. As a general matter, there would have to be some demonstration now on appeal that there was some prejudice, some actual prejudice. The theoretical possibility of that prejudice is not something upon which, in my submission, the Appeals Chamber should act. There may be some concern caused by the failure to make submissions which would cause this Court to exercise greater caution or scrutinise the record more carefully, but I wouldn't submit in a situation such as sentencing which is a highly discretionary matter by the Trial Chamber in which the Defence case has been clearly put forward and where the evidence has been called, for example, there have been testimony of witnesses who spoke about the acts of Blagojevic at the time, that he, for example, according to two witnesses, that he ordered his subordinates to check on the detainees at the Vuk Karadzic school. So there was evidence brought out as to general matters of his character or nature as a commander. Likewise, if the Court felt -- the Trial Chamber felt that there was sufficient concern in this regard, obviously there would be an obligation on that Trial Chamber to inquire as to whether there are any other matters that need to be brought forward. I would submit that one can assume that the Trial Chamber was not concerned as a result of the failure to file submissions on that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, I think it's now time to have a break, as scheduled. We are five minutes ahead, so I would suggest we come back at 10.15 instead of 10.20. We break for half an hour now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: We'll resume now the hearing, and I will give the floor to the Defence of Blagojevic for their reply for 20 minutes. You have the floor, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will try to limit myself to what my learned friend said in his response, and I hope I shall be able to cover everything I have noted. The first point is that this Appeals Chamber handed down decisions at one period of time; however, it has been misstated that this was in December 2003 and that the decision was published on the 7th of November. However, this was in September 2003. The decision and the grounds for the decision were published on the 7th of November, but it was actually in September 2003 that the Chamber issued this decision and it was only a few months after the start of trial. As regards the reference to the material from the media, I only wish to say that the fact that the article I quoted was published in the media, and the fact that it was published only a few days after the accusation of the 16th of July, when Mr. Karnavas made the accusation in nine paragraphs that this was an attempt at fee splitting, is something that could not have been obtained from the accused. We do not know how this information reached the media in fact. The issue of the reasons for the lack of cooperation between Mr. Karnavas and Mr. Blagojevic and the refusal to communicate is one where I wish to state that it was not only a breakdown in communication that happened, what started as a conflict concerning the co-counsel in late 2002, quite a bit earlier as can be seen from the Status Conferences held at the time, escalated into a conflict and the accused Blagojevic said that he felt that Mr. Karnavas was sabotaging the preparation of his defence. And this came to a head when he brought Mr. ^ Schifanelli as a military expert who was supposed to provide an expert opinion. This was only a few days before the dismissal, and on the 7th of April, 2003, he finally decided to dismiss his counsel, believing at the time and not being conversant with the law and having an opportunity to consult any lawyers, that it was up to him to choose. Because when he was brought to the Detention Unit, he then chose Mr. Karnavas as his counsel and his choice was confirmed by the Registry, which is how it came about that Mr. Karnavas was his Defence counsel. He felt that after everything that had happened, he also had the right to dismiss this counsel and did not have to communicate with him any further. What we wish to point out is that it was not the accused who brought about this crisis in relations with his counsel, that he did not bring the situation on himself. After the sabotage of his defence and the conflicts regarding the co-counsel, the refusal to have a co-counsel from Belgrade chosen by Mr. Blagojevic, matters came to a head when he was accused of attempting to commit a crime, when his counsel accused him of being a criminal. This totally destroyed their relationship, and Mr. Blagojevic cannot be blamed for this. After this, he could not have a shred of confidence in his counsel or try to communicate with him. I noted that the impossibility to communicate has not been established, but I have already stated that because of the nature of the relations between the two communication was no longer possible and it was not possible for Mr. Blagojevic to have confidence in his counsel. Raising the example of Momir Nikolic and his objection to his counsel is something that has nothing to do with this case, nor can it be used as an analogy in this case because the situation there was completely different. As for the objection that there was a miscarriage of justice because of the silence of the Defence, in conducting the case, what did Mr. Karnavas do to bring about a miscarriage of justice. Through his selection of evidence and the manner of presenting the case, I feel that in the total absence of any communication, no Defence counsel, not just Mr. Karnavas, but no other Defence counsel could have conducted the proceedings, cross-examining Prosecution witnesses, calling Defence witnesses and examining them, without the knowledge and agreement of the accused. Mr. Blagojevic, let me repeat, asked me to present only his first ground of appeal and did not give him much assistance in trying to learn more and get more information. Let me remind Your Honours, however, of the examples I have cited of instances very detrimental to Mr. Blagojevic, apart from this overall damage done to him which I've already mentioned. Among these is the military expert Mr. Schifanelli and his testimony regarding the tasks of the Bratunac Brigade, the area in which it was active, the actions taken by various persons and what they were able to do. All this was not dealt with properly by a proper military expert who would have testified at the trial. Mr. Karnavas proposed calling a certain Mr. Keserovic who was a security officer in a higher command, in the commands in the chain of command dealing with counter-intelligence and Momir Nikolic matters not concerning the brigade. He should have been a Defence witness, and he destroyed what had already been demonstrated; for example, the instructions of the General Staff from the year 1994, the directive that the job of a security officer in the brigade amounted to only 20 per cent of his overall work and that 80 per cent of his work was to communicate with the higher-level commands in the security organ, and that this applied to Momir Nikolic. It should have been shown that both in Potocari and in Bratunac and anywhere else, Momir Nikolic was acting on orders from the security chain of command, not in line with the 20 per cent of his activities; however, witness Keserovic changed this ratio to the detriment of the accused. And as for the men whom Mr. Blagojevic allegedly sent to the school to check what was going on, it's true that there was a protected witness who was a suspect at the time who said that he had been there but he didn't see anything bad happening and that he did not report this to Blagojevic; however, this was a Prosecution witness. Mr. Karnavas called witness Beatovic, who in his first statement never mentioned that Blagojevic had ever told him to go and see what was happening at the school, but when he appeared to testify, he said that he went there and saw nothing or nothing that would indicate that there were murders or beatings going on and that he went home and never reported to Mr. Blagojevic. Regardless of the value of such testimony, these are only a few examples that I myself noticed, as Mr. Blagojevic did not want to cooperate on this topic, but I have found examples where what was done at trial was to the detriment of Mr. Blagojevic. In April 2003, efforts were made to solve this problem. There were contacts between the Registry and the accused, and his standpoint was always consistent. But in June 2003, something happened that Mr. Blagojevic could not overlook. When he's given the chance, he will probably say something about this himself. With respect to the allegations made by the Prosecution that it is not true with respect to Blagojevic's testimony that he refused the possibility of testifying, this is not correct. He refused to be examined by Mr. Karnavas, whom he did not recognise as his Defence counsel. He did, however, wish to testify under oath, but he did not wish to be examined by Mr. Karnavas. And that also answers the question put by Her Honour Judge Vaz. Blagojevic, if I understand correctly from the transcript, spoke about a meeting with Mr. Karnavas - I apologise if I did not understand this correctly - or even two meetings. But from the beginning of April 2003 to this date, there has never been a meeting between Mr. Blagojevic and Mr. Karnavas. So when the issue of Blagojevic testifying arose - and for this reason, the trial was adjourned - the Registry did try to establish contact, but Mr. Blagojevic was already convinced, after everything that had happened, the accusations, the sabotage of his defence, did not wish to meet Mr. Karnavas. It's true that Mr. Karnavas said that he would not advise Mr. Blagojevic to testify; that was his professional advice. Many counsel before this Tribunal believe that their clients should not testify and that this is not in their best interests, but the reason Mr. Blagojevic did not testify was not because Mr. Karnavas gave this advice. He wished to testify, regardless of whether his testimony is seen as detrimental to his case or not. He wishes to testify. Therefore, this has been misinterpreted. With respect to the -- what was said about the interlocutory appeal and whether an accused who disagrees with his counsel should represent himself, Mr. Blagojevic did ask whether he could represent himself, but it was not possible for him to make such a decision. He said that he certainly needed a Defence lawyer, but a Defence lawyer who could prepare a proper defence, and that was the standpoint by which he abided. My time, I believe, is running out, so I wish to conclude by saying that in the Prosecutor's response to the first ground, attempts were made to show that Blagojevic himself interrupted communication with his counsel and worked against his own Defence; however, this was a complete breakdown of communication, making it impossible to cooperate because of the accusations that were made. After the serious accusation was made, no further contact was possible until the end of the trial. In my view, this really was not conducive to a fair trial, and for this reason, Mr. Blagojevic did not have a fair trial. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Domazet. This concludes the arguments on the appeal submitted by Mr. Blagojevic. We will move on now to the appeal of Mr. Jokic, and I will give the floor to the Defence of Mr. Jokic for their submissions for -- you have -- Mr. Murphy, you have one hour and ten minutes. That is -- well, until 11.45. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. And I will use the time, I hope, constructively not to necessarily address each and every ground of appeal, but to give Your Honours the assistance I can perhaps on the most difficult of the issues. [Interpretation] I would like to ask Judge Vaz in French --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Too fast for the French translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Vaz and Judge Guney could you let me know. [In English] Your Honours, I want to say, if I may, a few words by way of introduction, firstly, that I'm very conscious of the fact that this appeal relates to the events of Srebrenica, and so is Mr. Dragan Jokic. We are conscious of the fact that in the -- against the background of what has been described as the -- perhaps the worst event of its kind since the Second World War, we are nonetheless addressing Your Honours on a number of legal matters, one of two of which may perhaps at times appear to be of a technical nature. But I'm sure Your Honours will understand that even in this context and perhaps especially in this context, there is a need for precision and a need to be just to the accused who have been charged with and convicted of such serious crimes. And if the Trial Chamber made legal errors in convicting them of such crimes, then it's our submission that, regardless of the gravity of the matter, that is a matter which Your Honours have a duty to correct, and it will be our submission that the Trial Chamber in this case did make, in Mr. Jokic's case, at least two significant legal errors which require the reversal of his convictions. I also want to mention and to begin by thanking Your Honours for giving us leave at a relatively late stage of the proceedings, when I took over as lead counsel, to amend the notice of appeal and the appellant brief. Your Honours, I'm conscious that because of the Appeals Chamber's order, we -- we had to leave in the brief a significant quantity of material that had been included in the original brief. All I say is that if I had begun at the beginning and drafted it from the beginning, it might have been a different document, and the grounds of appeal might today have been a little different. Nonetheless, I'm confident that the leave that Your Honours did give us had enabled us to put the appeal into a context where it can be fully argued in the interests of justice and fairness to Mr. Jokic. And I do appreciate Your Honours' indulgence. The last thing I say by way of introduction is to remind Your Honours that on the 2nd of August of this year, we also filed a motion to strike or require redrafting of parts of the Prosecution's response brief. That, of course, was a step which we did not take lightly, and even though that motion was denied, I will invite Your Honours not to forget it entirely and to give some attention in preparing your judgement to the appendix to that motion in which we set out in a form of a table a number of parts of the Prosecution brief in which the Prosecution purported to describe the Trial Chamber's findings about what Mr. Jokic actually did. It was our position in that motion, Your Honours, and it is our position today, that those passages seriously misrepresent the Trial Chamber's actual findings. Excuse me, Your Honour, I think I need to make an adjustment here. For reasons that will be apparent in a moment, I need the assistance of the computer here. Your Honour, it's of great importance to our appeal to -- that the -- that the Appeals Chamber understand the actual factual basis on which the Trial Chamber made its decision to convict; and, as we set out in our motion, that was a very different basis from the basis upon which the Prosecution say the convictions were based. And I think when we come to discuss the detailed grounds of appeal, I think it will become clear to Your Honours why it is very important to understand what the basis of the conviction was, factually speaking. I have no doubt that the Prosecution, even in this hearing today, will once again invite the Appeals Chamber to take a much broader view of the Trial Chamber's findings than the Trial Chamber itself did. And so with the assistance of the Legal Officer, I think if Your Honours can be switched into e-court mode we can -- I'd like to provide just a visual summary of what is going on. If I can ask whether Your Honours now have access to that. Good. It should be on your screens. If Your Honours share my own terror and bewilderment at modern technology, I can re-assure you that this will be a very brief presentation. Hopefully, it will not take too long. All right. Well, I don't -- perhaps we can get one of the technical officers to assist. I'm not sure why that's not working. I was following the instructions I was given -- oh, there we go. I'm grateful to Ms. Lindsay. The basic finding that the Trial Chamber made in summary of the different allegations was expressed in paragraph 770 of the judgement, in which the Trial Chamber found that "Dragan Jokic rendered practical assistance which had a substantial effect on the commission of the mass executions in Orahovac, Pilica/Branjevo Military Farm, and Kozluk. His acts of assistance included coordinating, sending, and monitoring the deployment of Zvornik Brigade resources and equipment to the mass execution sites between 14 and 17th of July ..." The Prosecution has emphasised the word "included" in that paragraph as indicating that the Trial Chamber only mentioned those particular acts as being part of the assistance rendered by Mr. Jokic, but when we look at the Trial Chamber's other findings, it becomes clear that that was in fact the sum total of their findings about his criminal conduct. Now, that doesn't mean that the Trial Chamber did not make other findings about his activities during the 14th and 17th of July, and the Appeals Chamber having studied the briefs of the parties will have read about his role as duty officer and so on. But when it came to their findings as to culpability, it was to these acts and these acts alone that the Trial Chamber said these were acts of practical assistance that had a substantial effect on the commission. And that, of course, was a finding that had to be made because that was the actus reus of aiding and abetting. Now, the language that the Prosecution used in its response brief - I won't go through it all - but it included extravagant phrases such as that Mr. Jokic was involved in a central role; that the perpetrators relied on knowing that he would assist them; that he had overall knowledge of the murder operation; and so on and so forth. We've set it all out in our motion. If those had been the findings of the Trial Chamber, then one has to ask: Why did the Trial Chamber not agree with the Prosecution that Jokic was a part of the joint criminal enterprise?
