If his -- if he played a central role, if he was an officer of senior rank who had overall knowledge of the murder operation, was involved from start to finish over a period of four days - and this is all in the Prosecution's brief - why did they not find, as seemed inevitable, that he was part of a joint criminal enterprise? An allegation that they made before the Trial Chamber but have not pursued before this Appeals Chamber. On the screen before Your Honours now are the findings of the Trial Chamber on that issue. Paragraph 23, he did not have the requisite intent. 724: "The Trial Chamber finds that the appropriate form of liability is ... aiding and abetting." Paragraph 725: "The Trial Chamber finds that Dragan Jokic did not commit" these offences "as part of a joint criminal enterprise." And then lastly, the summary of the findings for the purposes of sentences in paragraph 836. As Your Honours know, the jurisprudence of the Tribunal is that sentencing must be based upon the overall criminality of the accused, and this is the Trial Chamber's statement of that criminality. And it begins by saying that Jokic, like Blagojevic, "did not play a major role in the commission of the crimes." That was the Trial Chamber's conclusion. For all the Prosecution's language about his overall involvement, his senior rank, being involved from start to finish, the perpetrators relying on Mr. Jokic, almost giving the impression that none of this would have happened if Mr. Jokic hadn't been there ready and willing to assist, what does the Trial Chamber actually say? He "did not play a major role." And in conclusion, they repeat what they had said in paragraph 770, that he substantially assisted by sending machinery, the Engineering Company, to the execution sites. Now, I will not take the time of the Trial Chamber to go through the other findings that we set forth in our motion. We demonstrated how, in other paragraphs of the judgement, the Trial Chamber also dismissed other allegations that had been made against Mr. Jokic. I needn't take Your Honours' time with that. I think we'll fast-forward through and now -- yeah, don't worry about that. Just fast-forward through that whole thing for me, please. Here we have one or two facts that I'm going to ask Your Honours to bear in mind later about the sites to which the Trial Chamber referred. Orahovac, it is alleged that Mr. Jokic had sent an excavator to that site at around noon. The killings began at that site during the early evening. And if time remains, I will address Your Honours about the implication of that finding at a later stage. In relation to the Pilica and Branjevo site, which is the subject of our sixth ground of appeal, Your Honours will see that here the executions had begun and ended during -- certainly at the latest the Trial Chamber found by 4.00 on the afternoon of the 16th of July. A request for machinery was received at 2210, and a second request early the next morning. The significance of that finding I will be dealing with very shortly. And then finally, as to Kozluk, once again we see that executions had ended, and then later machinery was sent. And I will again come back to the significance of that. I don't want to take too much time now. Now, Your Honour, I have no doubt the Prosecution will -- and we can go back to the transcript now. Thank you for that technical assistance; it's very much appreciated. I have no doubt that the Prosecution will give Your Honours their own version of the facts again, and I may have more to say in reply to that, but I'd like now, if I may, to come to the legal grounds of appeal, and these are really the third, fourth, and fifth grounds. To some extent, these grounds run together and constitute a sequence of grounds of appeal, and I will try, in order to be coherent, to deal with them in that way, certainly the third and fourth grounds. The third and fourth grounds, Your Honour, really relate to the subject of the law about aiding and abetting, as it has been set out in Article 7(1) of our Statute and also as it has been developed in the Tribunal's jurisprudence. Now, the important thing, as the Trial Chamber correctly recognised, and the Trial Chamber, we submit, correctly defined aiding and abetting and said that it required that the acts of the accused have a substantial effect on the commission of the offences. And in addressing this ground, Your Honour, I'm really now referring to Pilica and Branjevo Farm and Kozluk. The fourth ground adds to that, that if the assistance given by the accused was ex post facto, in other words, if it occurred at a time when the offences had already been committed and completed, then that cannot amount to aiding and abetting under the law of the Tribunal, under the Statute and the case law. And it really comes down to this in summary, that aiding and abetting is a form of commission. It is one of the ways in which offences may be committed or perpetrated. And so, if the assistance is rendered after the commission and completion of the offences, it follows from that that it is then too late for practical assistance to be rendered in the commission, in the commission, of the offences, which is, as the Trial Chamber correctly found, the definition of aiding and abetting in the Statute and also the way in which the cases have been developed in the Tribunal. Now, we have set out our analysis of the cases and the Statute, and the Prosecution responded. And I refer you particularly to paragraph 11.17 of the Prosecution's response brief. And it really appeared from the discussion in the two briefs that the -- the only real area of difference between the parties on the definition of the law was whether or not the Trial Chamber was correct in holding that the acts of the accused must be specifically directed towards the commission of the crimes. And I suppose, actually, then there was a second -- there was actually a second difference where the Trial Chamber also held, correctly, we say, that where the assistance given is ex post facto, that can only amount to aiding and abetting if there was a prior agreement between the accused and the perpetrators to render that assistance. In other words, if Mr. Jokic had on a prior -- at a prior time said in effect, If you need it, I will be there to help. If he had made that tacit or explicit agreement with the perpetrators at the outset. But as the Trial Chamber correctly noted, the law of the Tribunal is that the Prosecution would have to prove the existence of such a prior agreement in order to convict Jokic on these facts. Because remember what happened, Your Honours, in the two cases we referred to of Pilica and Kozluk. Clearly, there can be really no dispute about this, the offences were entirely over, completed, done with, before Mr. Jokic even arguably rendered an act of assistance to the perpetrators. Now, Orahovac is a separate case. I'll come back to that one if I have time. But in relation to those two cases that I mentioned, clearly, the law of the Tribunal is, as the Trial Chamber correctly found, was -- is that the -- firstly, the acts of the accused must be specifically directed, they must be -- render practical assistance in the commission of the crimes, in the commission of the crimes. And that if the assistance is ex post facto, then that cannot amount to aiding and abetting unless there was a prior agreement. And we would submit, Your Honour, that the fact -- once the Trial Chamber decided that the Prosecution had failed to prove that Mr. Jokic was a member of the joint criminal enterprise, there was no other evidence of any prior agreement at all between that -- between Mr. Jokic and the perpetrators. Now, the -- what does the Prosecution say about this? Well, firstly, they say that specifically directed should not be regarded as an element -- as a separate element of aiding and abetting, that's at paragraph 11.17 of their brief. We replied to that at paragraphs 36 to 39 of our reply, and we showed that in fact the consistent line of authority in the Tribunal from Tadic onwards has been -- does exactly support the Trial Chamber's finding in that respect. They stated the law as it has been laid down in a series of cases. And the Prosecution supplies no authority, really, to contradict that. Moreover, the Prosecution agrees with us that the substantial effect of the accused's acts must be related to the commission of the offence itself. The Prosecution, in paragraph 11.9, then invites the Appeals Chamber in essence to jettison the Trial Chamber's findings and say, Well, regardless of what the Trial Chamber found, the Appeals Chamber has power to substitute its own findings and therefore to substitute its own view for that of the Trial Chamber. And I know that Your Honours will agree that that's the sort of thing that an Appeals Chamber should not do lightly and not without a significant record. And, Your Honour, the record on appeal here, the Trial Chamber's findings based on evidence is very clear. There is no basis for saying that they got it wrong. And, Your Honours, I would submit that the Trial Chamber's factual findings in that regard should be respected here. We also demonstrated, Your Honour, in relation to the fourth ground, that not only is our point on ex post facto good law in this Tribunal, but it really represents the view across the board in domestic systems of law. And although I know that is a second reconsideration, it is significant here because it seems that right across the board, both in common law and continental systems, the same principle applies. And Your Honours will see in paragraphs 150 and following of our brief, we set out the law in a number of jurisdictions, including the former Yugoslavia and England. And we showed that there was a separate offence in these jurisdictions. In England, it would have been called in the old days being an accessory after the fact, where this offence is committed where a crime has already been completed and then after that the accused comes, in some way, to the aid of the perpetrators. And both at common law and by Statute and I think also in the continental penal codes that were examined, the same principle applies expressed in -- sometimes in a little different language, that this was a separate offence, being an accessory after the fact. The problem the Prosecution faces, Your Honours, is that that offence does not appear in Article 7(1) of the Tribunal, the Statute. For what reason, I cannot really enlighten Your Honours very much. We drew attention in our brief to the fact that the International Law Commission had made some observations about how that offence should be treated; they made certain recommendations I think pertaining to what should be the position of the Statute of the International Criminal Court. But be that as it may, clearly for some reason, consciously, the decision was taken not to include an offence similar to being an accessory after the fact in Article 7(1) of our Statute; it simply isn't there. And in our submission, Your Honour, that is fatal to the conviction of Mr. Jokic for any offences regarding the Pilica/Branjevo site or the Kozluk site because of the undisputed evidence. And if one looks at it -- if one takes every finding that the Trial Chamber made at face value and puts it in favour of the Prosecution, one sees immediately that whatever assistance Mr. Jokic gave was clearly ex post facto and he simply, as a matter of law, Your Honours, cannot be convicted on that basis. Those convictions were simply wrong as a matter of law. Now, I will -- there is -- well, one other thing, Your Honour, that I should say at this point. And this will now lead me into the fifth ground, but it's of ongoing importance in relation to Mr. Jokic's overall liability. The Trial Chamber accepted that Mr. Jokic had nothing to do with any acts of reburial of the bodies after the immediate aftermath of the massacres. Now, clearly there is a qualitative difference between the initial burying of the bodies and any reburial because it's hard to avoid the conclusion that a reburial could have had only one purpose and that would have been to prevent the detection of these crimes by investigators. And that leads me on to the fifth ground of appeal, which was one that Your Honours gave us leave to insert and found that if true it would make a difference in the outcome of the appeal, which I respectfully agree. It was a matter that was raised in passing in the original appellant brief, but Ms. Loukas and I took the view that it was important enough to be discussed in its own right. And in coming to this fifth ground of appeal, I want to reiterate, Your Honour, that nothing that I'm about to say in any way at all indicates any disrespect for the victims or anything less than the horror which both I and Mr. Jokic feel for what happened at Srebrenica -- in regard to Srebrenica. But we must face facts about what happened here. Now, we've raised a certain number of factual challenges to the Trial Chamber's conclusions, but for the moment, I want to put all of those aside and I want to ask Your Honours to join me in just a theoretical construct in which we assume for the moment that everything that the Prosecution said and alleged about Mr. Jokic was true, assume that he knew what was going on, and that with full knowledge of that he nonetheless deployed equipment of the Engineering Company to the three sites in order to enable the bodies to be buried. Now, making that assumption, Your Honours, I, with the greatest respect, pose this question: What else was Mr. Jokic to do? Because unlike the reburial, and there really is no excuse for that. There is no way to explain that in innocent terms at all. But the initial burial, Your Honours, was something that simply had to be done. If Mr. Jokic had not done it, somebody else had to. It was a matter of -- as the President said in introducing the ground, a matter of public health, but whichever language you choose to put on it, it was simply inevitable. Well, the Prosecution, in its brief, says that well it doesn't matter what Mr. Jokic's motivation may have been, but this is not a matter of motivation. It's a matter of the actus reus. It's a matter of whether what he did in these hypothetical circumstances, as I'm portraying them to be, making these assumptions that we do not really agree with, but making these assumptions, it is a matter of whether or not that was an act of assistance. And the legal issue involved, Your Honours, is the burden of proof. The Prosecution had the burden of proving that Jokic committed an unlawful act, and that that was an act of practical assistance to the perpetrators, having a substantial commission -- effect on the commission of the offence. But it was an equally probable inference from the evidence that what Mr. Jokic did simply had to be done regardless of the horrific crimes that had resulted in this situation. And if that is true, if that logically is the position, the Prosecution failed to discharge the burden of proof, to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Jokic committed the actus reus of aiding and abetting. Now, if Your Honours feel that that is a technicality that is inappropriate here, you will, please, blame me for that and not Mr. Jokic, because, as his counsel, it's my responsibility to advance grounds of appeal. But it was my judgement and is my judgement that that is a ground of appeal that Your Honours have to consider here seriously, because as a matter of policy, it raises an issue as to what conduct one criminalises in the aftermath of a situation created by the criminal conduct of others. And it may not be the first time that this problem is being posed, and it certainly probably will not be the last. And it may be something that the Appeals Chamber feels that it would be good to lay down some principle about for the guidance of future Prosecutors and Courts. Where does one draw the line and say criminality begins here? The Prosecution would say, Well, Jokic was on any view doing something that he shouldn't have done, and they raise the issue that the fact that his act may have been lawful in itself does not prevent it from amounting to aiding and abetting. We agree with that, Your Honour. It's not -- we don't contend that one cannot aid and abet by means of an act which is, per se, and in itself lawful. And the Prosecution in fact gave a number of examples in their response brief as to situations in which they felt that that would be true. At paragraph 13.14, they gave a number of examples, including one involving General Krstic, as Your Honours may recall. Now, one can argue as to whether those examples involved lawful or unlawful conduct, but I want to make it clear that we don't disagree with the Prosecution in principle, that certainly a lawful act may amount to aiding and abetting. But we would also add to that that it must be an act of assistance. If it's an act that has to be done to redress the immediate consequences of crimes committed by others and if in this case the consequences of leaving it undone would have been to render very much worse the situation that was already bad, then the question I invite Your Honours to give some thought to is: Should that conduct in principle be regarded as criminal conduct? I submit that that's a question that should be faced and resolved, and I suggest that it should be resolved in favour of Mr. Jokic in the particular circumstances of this case based upon the situation regarding the burden of proof. Your Honours, I have very little time remaining, so with your permission, I would like to use it in this way, to address in general terms the question of mens rea which is the subject of our first and second grounds of appeal. And I will -- rather than go through the very lengthy evidence that's been presented on both sides of this issue in the brief - and Your Honours will be very much aware of - I can perhaps do it in this way. And I recognise that I face here the -- the burden of persuading Your Honours not only that the Trial Chamber came to the wrong decision, but that it was a decision that no reasonable Trial Chamber could have reached. In each case -- in each case that we have alluded to, the three different sites, the evidence of mens rea against Mr. Jokic was necessarily circumstantial. There was no direct evidence. It depended upon inferences that were to be drawn from the circumstances. And if we may take Orahovac as an example, that was of course a situation in which it was alleged that Mr. Jokic sent equipment to the site significantly before any killings took place at that site. The evidence, Your Honours, was - and I think this is not really disputed - that on no occasion did Mr. Jokic ever give an order that indicated knowledge that any killings were to take place. There was clearly evidence to support an inference that he knew there were prisoners and that he knew prisoners were being detained; that's clear. He was involved, the Trial Chamber found, for example, in sending men to guard prisoners. But as far as sending equipment, the Prosecution relies only on inferences that they say should have been drawn from the evidence. Jokic did not give orders to anyone to go and participate in burials; that much is clear. What happened was that when the vehicles got to the sites in question, they were used for that purpose. And the question is: Was it appropriate for the Trial Chamber to draw the conclusion that Mr. Jokic must have known and did know the true purpose for which they were being sent. Take Orahovac, for example. Hours before, on the Prosecution's own case, any killings were to be committed at that site. On what basis could the Trial Chamber have found that Mr. Jokic had knowledge? In the case of the Pilica site, the situation is even more interesting, as Your Honours will see from our specific ground of appeal, because in that instance, there was actually no evidence that Mr. Jokic personally ordered the equipment at all. In fact, the evidence was that the orders were given by others, and the involvement of Mr. Jokic in that is an inference upon an inference that somehow Mr. Jokic not only knew what was going on but knew what orders other people, outside any chain of command he was involved in, had given. Your Honour, I'm not going to try to develop that because the evidence is very detailed and it's there. And rather than give Your Honours a necessarily hurried and garbled account, I will leave that. And I think at this point, Your Honour, I will invite any questions from the Bench on the submissions I've made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, counsel. Judge Shahabuddeen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Murphy, somewhere in your lucid submissions you might have referred to your client being accused of aiding and abetting in respect of the aftermath of a completed crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what I want to ask your attention to is page 30 -- 305 of the record. It says there that the accused Dragan Jokic is found guilty pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute through aiding and abetting on the following counts: Count 2, extermination as a crime against humanity. Now, if that is a correct reading of the trial record, then I have to ask you whether you would be inclined to draw a distinction between the completion of a discrete single crime, such as murdering a man, and the extermination of whole battalions of souls. They've got to be buried, I take it, and whether one puts that on the basis that the legality of the act is foreseen as completely lawful, separate and apart, it's another question whether it is seen as participating in the fullness of the act, the criminal act, of exterminating whole battalions of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do recognise that distinction, and in fact I think we did make it at one point either in our brief or in our reply. I can't give Your Honour a paragraph reference now, but I can find it. I think we mentioned that in any event, even if the Court was against us on the general principle, it seemed clear, that as regards the crime of murder, the conviction would have to be reversed because on any view that crime was -- was completed. But, Your Honour, having made that distinction, I would say that we maintain our argument in regard to each of the convictions for this reason: Although, of course, these are very different crimes and once -- one can only sympathise both with the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber in trying to give legal definition to events of this magnitude and this horror and whatever definition they give to them, Your Honour, in some ways, obviously, is not entirely adequate to describe what happened. And I take Your Honour's point that when one talks of extermination, that might have a broader impact than the crime of murder per se. But as a realistic matter, what was it that was alleged here? By the time that Mr. Jokic became involved in any way, the whole joint criminal enterprise had been plotted and completed, starting not just with the killings but, as Your Honour knows, with the overrunning of the United Nations safe area in Srebrenica, the expulsion of the Muslim population, the unlawful detention, the other ill treatment that was carried out. And in all of that picture, I think Your Honour could rightly regard as part of the crime of extermination. And obviously, that crime was much broader in its scope than simply the act of murder, and we of course accept that. But the fact is, Your Honour, that even the crime of extermination at some point comes to an end. And realistically, one would say -- I would submit that where the crime of extermination ends in this case is co-extensive with the acts of murder, because after that, the criminality had in fact ended and what was -- the act of burial -- and again, Your Honour, I don't take any great point on whether that was lawful or unlawful. My fifth ground was based upon the fact that it was just necessary. And in relation to the third and fourth grounds, Your Honour, the ground of ex post facto, once again, even for extermination, one is caught with this dilemma that there is, if you will, a lacuna in the Statute, whether consciously or otherwise, that the offense committed in these circumstances at Pilica and Kozluk is simply not there. It's an act of accessory after the fact and it's simply not in Article 7(1) of the Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I'm so grateful, Mr. Murphy. May I press you on another point? We have here reference at page 305 of the trial record to murder in Count 4. Well, that invites the imagination to a single murder or two or three or four, but is that the case here? Count 3 and Count 4 in the indictment before we -- reads this way: "By their acts and omissions described in the preceding paragraphs, Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic committed Count 3, murder, and Count 4, murder." So again, we are on the field of visualising not a single murder, but murder of whole fields of humanity. Now, would that enterprise be considered as concluded in its criminality unless the bodies were buried?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me first, if I may, respectfully offer one -- just a slight point, Your Honour. In fact, the Trial Chamber did not convict Mr. Jokic on Count 3 because they found that -- I think that that would have been cumulative --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Count 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: But Your Honour's point of course applies equally to Count 4. And in that regard, Your Honour, I would say, yes. If one looks at the offence of murder -- and that's really why I agree with Your Honour's distinction between murder and extermination -- because if one looks at the crime of murder as defined, I would submit that it is clearly complete the moment the act of killing has ended. And although, as Your Honour says, and this is a case in which unfortunately we all have to exercise our imaginations in a horrific way, but I would respectfully submit that the fact that murder was committed on this scale does not affect the point of principle that we make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You see, the point which emerges from the indictment is that the counts for murder relate to the count for extermination. If thousands of people were exterminated under Count 2, then they would equally be regarded as having been murdered under Count 4. So it's not the same as a case in which an accused person is indicted for murdering a discrete person, thousands of persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's true. And I think in a way the problem comes from the fact that in the Statute of the Tribunal we combine a number of different offences derived from different sources of law. So in one respect, we have violations of the laws and customs of war, we have crimes against humanity, and then of course, potentially, we could have violations of the Geneva Conventions. Your Honour, the -- and of course, that's one reason why we've developed the rules that we have about cumulative convictions. But those rules, as Your Honour knows, really going back at least to the Celebici case, where Judge Hunt in his separate opinion wrote a very detailed account of the rules of cumulative convictions, we've limited that concept to a rather technical overlapping test to see whether there are additional elements. And when one looks at the counts in this indictment, we see that clearly some of them do not fit within that cumulative test. Nonetheless, though, they still refer to the same factual background. And the -- although the Prosecution, quite rightly, charges an accused with each offence which they think can be supported by the evidence, at the end of the day, when we look at the convictions, we see that there is an overall criminal act relating to a certain factual situation. And that's reflected, I think, in the decision of the Trial Chamber to impose a single offence reflecting the totally of all the crimes for which Jokic was convicted. And we would say, Your Honour, that however one describes these crimes, they came to an end at a certain point. And in relation to Pilica or Kozluk, that point was clearly many hours before Jokic on any view became involved. And that's really the basis of our third and fourth grounds of appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I thank you for your assistance Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, President. Mr. Murphy, you spoke earlier about the war situation that would arise if the burials would not take place. Did you refer to a compelling public health necessity to have the burials quickly or to something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- we did in our brief suggest that they -- the -- clearly there was such a danger presented. We referred to evidence that had been presented to the Trial Chamber, and I don't -- it's such a distasteful phrase, but it was called terrain restoration. I've stayed away from that phrase because it's distasteful. There was evidence presented to the Trial Chamber that justified the finding -- would have justified a finding that there was an imminent public health danger. The Prosecution, in its brief, complained that we were raising a new issue. Your Honour, in some respects perhaps, but we pointed out in reply that it was really the -- simply the issue of burden of proof, that there was in fact evidence on the record from which the Trial Chamber could have inferred that the acts of burial were a necessity. And I think that's a matter that the Trial Chamber or this Appeals Chamber could really take judicial notice. It's simply a reality of the situation that was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Murphy. Let me see whether I understand. Apart from the legal arguments that you adduced on aiding and abetting and the temporal element, you seem to be saying two things and correct me if I'm wrong: That first, Jokic did not have knowledge of the killings; and second, his acts were based on public health or necessity. If that is so, do tell me which is your primary argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I perhaps didn't make as clear as I should have. In relation to the fifth ground of appeal, I was asking Your Honours to make a set of assumptions. I did not represent to the Court, either in brief or in oral argument, that this was Mr. Jokic's motivation. The position we have taken was that if we make every assumption that the Prosecution asked the Trial Chamber to make, in other words, if we assumed that Mr. Jokic knew exactly what was going on and with that knowledge he dispatched equipment to carry out the burials, making all of those assumptions, we say that the Prosecution still did not meet its burden of proof because there was an equally probable explanation consistent with innocence. But, Your Honour, again, I want to make very, very clear that for the purposes of the fifth ground, I'm making -- asking the Court to make assumptions as to the facts that we -- thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, I was making simply there -- asking Your Honours to make an assumption as to the theoretical construct within which making every assumption in favour of the Prosecution we say they did not meet the burden of proof. But on a factual issue, we certainly do think and submit that the Trial Chamber should not have found that Mr. Jokic had the knowledge or mens rea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. If there are no other questions, I would turn to the Prosecution and ask the Prosecution to submit their arguments in response for 30 minutes. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you. I will be addressing the factual challenges to the Trial Chamber's judgement in all of the appellant's grounds, but will attempt to group them thematically. It is our submission that the arguments raised by the appellant, in an attempt to demonstrate errors in the judgement are based on a misapprehension of the judgement or are simply unsustainable. A predominant theme, as we've heard today, is that the appellant's argument is his claim that the mass killings of which Jokic was convicted as an aider and abettor are distinct crimes separate and apart from the overall murder operation. A secondary argument that the appellant makes is that the initial mass burials in Kozluk and Branjevo Farm occurred after the commission of the crimes. First, I will address the argument that the Trial Chamber found the burials in Kozluk and Branjevo Military Farm mass killing sites after the commission of the crime; second, I will address his argument that the Trial Chamber only found him liable for individual acts of contribution; third, I will address his challenge to the Trial Chamber's finding that he substantially contributed to the murder operation on the facts as found, which he raises in ground 3 of his appeal; and finally, I will address the issue of knowledge, with time permitting. We largely rest on our brief in respect of ground 5 that -- in respect of ground 5, when addressing -- in respect to his claim that there was an equally innocent explanation that he carried out the burials to promote public health. But it's our position that there has been no shred of evidence presented at trial to support this claim. There has been no testimony whatsoever. He did not testify and he could have. It was never raised in argument at trial. He seems to be raising a hypothetical for the first time on appeal. Secondly, the standard is that he knowingly assisted the crimes. And as found by the Trial Chamber, he -- he did know that he assisted the crimes. The only alleged evidence that the -- that the appellant refers to is a reference to Article 21 of the Legal Act which applies to the civilian protection forces and was referred to by the Trial Chamber in relation to the Bratunac Brigade. It's not evidence that Mr. Jokic carried out the burials for the purpose of promoting health, and there's no basis for the assertion that Mr. Jokic had a duty to act as he did, nor that he even knew about such a duty. To the contrary, the evidence, based on the Trial Chamber's findings, was based on the totality of his acts under paragraph 770, including sending guards to detain prisoners and his conversations with -- and one of the primary implementers in the operation, Beara. Furthermore, the burials in Orahovac occurred while the mass killings were ongoing. So that's just to point out that there was absolutely no evidence to support this assertion. Your Honours, the crimes that were committed following the fall of Srebrenica were, as you know, on a vast and unimaginable scale. This was not a series of individual murders, one having nothing to do with the other, rather, it was an organised and continuous operation involving the mass killing of over 7.000 men and boys from Srebrenica over the course of four days and which followed a well-established pattern. The murder operation began with the separation of the men and boys in Potocari on 12 and 13 July, their capture from the column, their transportation to Zvornik on buses, their detention at schools, and ultimately their summary executions and their burials which occurred either during or immediately after the crimes. The Zvornik Brigade members were involved in every facet of this operation. Against that background, turning to the first question, has the appellant demonstrated that the Trial Chamber found that the Kozluk and Branjevo Farm initial burials occurred after the commission of the crimes. A reading of the judgement as a whole demonstrates that there were two central features to the operation: First, that it was a single murder operation which was ongoing and involved several components, and that is the capture, detention, mass killings, and burials; and secondly, that the burials were an essential component of the crime. So the appellant attempts to deconstruct the judgement by claiming that the Chamber found that the initial burials occurred after the commission of the crime. That's not what it found at all. If we look to paragraphs 291 under the heading "organised mass executions and burials," it found: "A wide-scale and organised killing operation carried out by the VRS and MUP from 12 to 19 July," and it found that "thousands of Bosnian Muslim men were executed and buried in different locations in Srebrenica, Bratunac, and Zvornik." And again, in the context of its findings on extermination, at paragraph 577, it found that: "The crimes were one murder operation which occurred -- which were carried out in a short time-period with a similar pattern of killings." In regards to its conclusions on the mass killings in paragraph 568, it referred to the burials that occurred either on or close to the execution site and concluded that considering the limited time-period in which all this happened, the Trial Chamber cannot but conclude that these killings were done in an organised way. So it's clear that the ongoing crimes followed a well-established pattern of mass killings and subsequently followed by mass burials, and that's in stark contrast --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: May you perhaps slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I will. And that's in stark contrast to its findings in the -- in respect of the reburials, which are found at paragraphs 730 to 31 of the judgement. The Chamber -- the Trial Chamber expressly distinguished between the reburials and initial burials by expressly finding that the reburials occurred not as a result of the murder operation, but as a consequence of the scrutiny of the international community a few months after the murder operation. And in fact, that -- those paragraphs, 730 and 31, which exclusively deal with the reburials, is the only place in the entire judgement which mentions ex post facto aiding and abetting. And it might assist the Chamber to be aware of how this matter was approached at trial. In the decision on the Defence motion for acquittal pursuant to 98 bis, the Trial Chamber made it clear that the reburials were part of the overall murder operation or -- the initial burials, rather, were part of the murder operation and only characterised the reburials as ex post facto aiding and abetting. The appellant, at that stage, at the trial stage did not challenge this characterisation. Had it not been clear, he could have challenged it then. Furthermore, the fact that the initial burials were part of the crime is supported by the evidence. Witness Erdemovic, who participated in the killings at Branjevo Farm, testified that the lieutenant-colonel who was present and overseeing those killings at the farm stated that the men who were being shot would be buried there, and that's in footnote 1309 of the judgement. Clearly, he anticipated the burials before the killings were over, because the burials were part of the crime. This evidence is also consistent with the events in Orahovac at mass killing site, where the burials occurred during the killings and the location of the grave had been premarked with wooden poles. There's no material difference between the killings and burials in Orahovac and the other sites. In fact, the same equipment and personnel were used in all three sites. Turning then to the second question: Has the appellant demonstrated that the Trial Chamber did not find that Mr. Jokic's act substantially contributed to the ongoing murder operation? First, as I have just indicated in various sections of the judgement, the Trial Chamber concluded that this was one ongoing murder operation which was carried out from 14 to 17 July, and included capture -- they included several components, which was the capture, the transfer, the detention, and the execution to burials. Each of these aspects was a component part of the operation. Second, the Trial Chamber found that Mr. Jokic substantially contributed to the crimes by his acts as both as duty officer and as chief of engineering, as reflected in its primary factual findings, which is combined with paragraph 770, in which the Chamber finds that his acts of assistance included coordinating, monitoring, and sending Zvornik Brigade resources. So when the appellant challenges the wording in paragraph 770, he is merely putting forward his own interpretation of the intention behind the Trial Chamber's language, which differs from the express language of paragraph 770. By doing so, the appellant is ignoring that the Trial Chamber expressly stated that his acts included coordinating and monitoring, not just sending engineering resources -- Zvornik Brigade resources and not just sending engineering resources. Third, the facts as found in the preliminary factual findings, for example, in paragraphs 325 to 326 and 347 of the judgement are acts of contribution which the Chamber expressly found. So although these acts substantially contributed to the overall murder operation and the Trial Chamber found that Mr. Jokic was aware of the ongoing killings since 14 July, the Trial Chamber did, in addition to that, look to his individual acts of contribution, though it was not required to do so. Further, the appellant ignores the findings of the Trial Chamber by looking to the sentencing paragraph out of context and claiming that the Trial Chamber did not find liability for all the other acts. It cannot be that all the other findings must be dismissed because of one paragraph in the sentencing context in the judgement. But even limiting his acts of contribution to individual sites, the Trial Chamber's findings included his acts as duty officer, as reflected in its primary factual findings in paragraph 770, so his acts of contribution are more than those submitted by the appellant. It wasn't just sending a piece of equipment, as the appellant claims, but his other acts such as assuring the integrity of the detentions and keeping a primary player in the operation informed of problems concerning the prisoners were part of his acts of contribution. Alternatively, even just on the acts of sending excavators to crime sites alone, the findings were sustainable because the burials were a component part of the ongoing crime for which he had knowledge when he sent equipment and men, and as duty officer and chief of engineering, he was coordinating and monitoring the burials. Lastly, if the Appeals Chamber finds that the Trial Chamber limited its findings to Jokic's acts of assistance to sending equipment to each site, then in our submission, the Trial Chamber erred by failing to take into account its own factual findings. And it is our submission that the Appeals Chamber can rely on those findings to find substantial contribution without disturbing the conviction. Your Honours, I'd like to turn to the third question which the appellant raises in his reply and, to some extent, raised this morning, and that is: Has the appellant demonstrated that on the facts as found the Trial Chamber was unreasonable in reaching the conclusion that he substantially contributed to the murder operation? The appellant attempts to diminish his liability by alleging that his acts were too remote or insubstantial, but in looking at the judgement as a whole, the Trial Chamber found that his acts as duty officer were part of a constellation of the acts which contributed to the murder operation. And that's clear from paragraph 770 which refers to coordinating, monitoring and sending of Zvornik Brigade resources. So in our submission, there was more than ample evidence upon which the Trial Chamber could find that he substantially contributed to the crimes and its findings were reasonable. First, as found by the Trial Chamber in paragraphs 324 to 326, as duty officer on 14 July, he acted on a request of Witness P130 to provide additional security to guard prisoners in Orahovac. And in doing so, Jokic substantially assisted the murder operation because the detention of thousands of prisoners in preparation of their simultaneous killings was an essential feature of the murder operation. So by maintaining the integrity of the detentions, he was ensuring the success of the mass killings. Second, he then contacted Beara, who was a primary implementer of the murder operation as found by the Trial Chamber, paragraph 321, and informed him of problems with the prisoners. By this point, there were thousands of prisoners detained in schools in Zvornik, and in particular, the mass killings in Orahovac were under way. So in the context of the number of resources needed to transport, guard, maintain control over them, and ultimately kill them, by keeping a major implementer of the operation informed of what is happening concerning the prisoners, he assisted the operation by ensuring that it would continue. This is particularly salient in light of having earlier informed former Drina Corps commander General Zivanovic about the large number of prisoners or the Bosnian Muslims in the Zvornik area. And then he informed General Miletic of the Main Staff of the movements of the Bosnian Muslims in the area and their surrender. Mr. Jokic knew of the murder operation, and in his role as duty officer, he continued to facilitate the ability of the VRS to deal with the onslaught of the Muslim column in the area, and he informed them of the surrender of the Muslims. He's thereby contributing to the operation by ensuring that the main players are kept informed of what was happening on the ground, which assists in ensuring that the operation can continue. It is also relevant that when Mr. Jokic informed Beara about problems with the prisoners, the murders in Orahovac were under way, and indeed there were problems with the mass executions, as prisoners were attempting to escape, as reflected in paragraph 329 of the judgement. Third, as the Chamber found in paragraph 347 of the judgement, Mr. Jokic prevented interference with the prisoners in Pilica by telling Pero Petrovic to mind his own business and that there were people taking care of this. He thereby assisted, once again, in maintaining the integrity of the detentions which ensured the success of the mass killings. Finally, he deployed engineering equipment and personnel to multiple killing sites where the mass burials were carried out, and it's our submission, that even on this evidence alone, the Trial Chamber's findings of his substantial contribution is reasonable because he didn't just send excavators to one or two sites, as the appellant alleges in his brief, but as the Trial Chamber found, he coordinated and monitored the mass burials. And those acts in themselves substantially contributed to the murder operation, as reflected in paragraph 770. The sequence of his acts, taken together with the Trial Chamber's findings, that in practice, as chief of engineering, Mr. Jokic issued orders to implement -- to implement the orders of the commander, that he had a de facto advisory role to members of the Engineering Company due to his engineering expertise, that he was tasked with the responsibility of overseeing the proper use of equipment demonstrates that he coordinated and monitored the burial operation. And I would just like to place a document up on the screen which itemises the Trial Chamber's findings as to the sequence of events or the sequence of his acts. If we -- if we look to his acts each day, starting from -- oh, I'm sorry. Your Honours, this is actually on e-court. I'm not sure if you're -- if you have it on your screens yet. Thank you. I'm -- I think it's now on e-court. If we look to his acts each day, Your Honour, starting from 14 July, it's clear that he was coordinating and monitoring the burials, as the Chamber found. On 14 July, after having sent additional guards to assist with the detentions in Orahovac, Mr. Jokic then sent Ristanovic, a member of the Engineering Company, with an excavator to Orahovac in the presence of deputy commander of engineering Bogicevic, who the Trial Chamber found consulted with Jokic on all matters, as found in paragraph 523. At Orahovac, Bogicevic instructed Ristanovic to dig at a premarked location. The killings were ongoing during the burials. Later, another engineer was sent to assist Ristanovic with the digging and he arrived at the site with deputy commander Bogicevic. During the night, one of the engineering excavators was used to shine a light on the killing fields, and at the end of the day, Jokic called Beara and told him about problems with the prisoners. The next day, on 15 July, platoon commander Lazarevic instructed Ristanovic to return to Orahovac to finish digging the grave. We know from other findings that Lazarevic replaced deputy commander Bogicevic in his absence. That's in footnote 1237. And we know from the Trial Chamber's findings and the sequence of events on 16 July, that as platoon commander, Lazarevic would report back to Jokic. The following day, on 16 day, after the killings occurred in Kozluk, between 15 and 16 July, Jokic sent two engineers to Kozluk and told them that they would get the necessary instructions at the site from the platoon commander Lazarevic. At the site, Lazarevic instructed them to cover up bodies who were -- that -- which were already dug -- in holes. About 30 minutes later, Mitrovic, one of the diggers, is replaced by a member of the Josanica company which was commandeered by the brigade for the use of the Engineering Company. Dragan Jokic knew that Mitrovic's excavator was not in working order when he sent him out initially to Kozluk. In the evening, Mr. Jokic was then informed of a request to send an excavator and a loader to be at the Branjevo Farm for the next day on 17 July. By this point, the killings had occurred in Branjevo Farm on 16 July. And on 17 July, at 8.00 a.m., once again, platoon commander Lazarevic instructed Ristanovic to go to Branjevo Farm with an excavator and at the site Lazarevic instructed Ristanovic to dig. These repeated successive acts of burials that are synchronised with the ongoing mass killings over a space of a few days can hardly be considered remote or insubstantial in the context of an ongoing mass execution. It was reasonable to find on these factual findings that Jokic was coordinating and monitoring the mass burials. These acts in themselves, when placed in context of his role as the duty officer and chief of engineering, substantially contributed to the mass killings, let alone when combined with his acts of further detentions and communicating with the primary players of the mass killings and the murder operation. Finally, Your Honours, I just want to deal with one -- with a couple of points in relation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: May I draw your attention, Ms. Issa, that you have three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I'll try and make my point in three minutes. Thank you, Your Honour. Just in respect of the issue of knowledge, it is our submission that the appellant has not demonstrated that the Trial Chamber was unreasonable in finding that Mr. Jokic knew about the murder operation. Most of our response is contained in our response brief in relation to the challenge of the -- of the factual findings. I do want to point out, in respect of sending Ristanovic to Orahovac on 14 July, in his reply, the appellant asserts that there was an absence of evidence. The question is whether the Trial Chamber's finding as to Jokic's knowledge of the mass killings when he sent Ristanovic was reasonable. In our submission, it was because it cannot -- he sent Ristanovic either during or right before the mass killings to a school full of prisoners in Orahovac. There is no legitimate purpose to send a digger with an excavator to a school full of prisoners in Orahovac, other than if he had not anticipated the burials in anticipation of the mass killings. So on this evidence alone, the evidence reflects that he knew, but certainly, the Chamber found, based on several bodies of evidence, as we state in our brief, that he was -- that he knew about the mass killings. Those conclude my submissions, Your Honours. I am available for questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. I turn to my colleagues. Judge Shahabuddeen has a question first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One little question, Ms. Issa. You will pardon me if I don't seem to recollect precisely the page in the trial judgement which I should be referring, but I have before me paragraph 129 of the trial judgement. The third line reads this way: "They tried to find shelter at the UN base in Srebrenica." My question is: Would you kindly point out where in the trial judgement there is an explanation of that phrase "the UN base in Srebrenica." Was there some special status assigned by the United Nations to this little town?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, if Your Honour -- yes, Your Honour. The answer is: Yes, that the town was -- that Srebrenica was considered to be a -- a protected enclave by the United Nations at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Is there somewhere in the trial judgement where that is made explicit? I appreciate that you cannot on the hoof, so to speak, point exactly to where it might be. Can you show us, show me, that it's someplace in the trial judgement?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: It's paragraph 100, Your Honour, and I thank my colleague for assisting me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: 100. Oh, yes, United Nations Security Council -- thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: If there are no other questions, then I believe we can adjourn for the day. We will reconvene tomorrow morning at 8.00 to listen to the reply of the Defence of Mr. Jokic. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
